# Hours, Output and the Pilot Problem: A Re-examination of the Halden Reduced-Hours Pilot

*Comment, Journal of Labour and Organisation Studies. K. Varga and T. Holm, Centre for Applied Labour Statistics.*

## Abstract

The Halden pilot reported that 61 organisations maintained output while cutting scheduled hours by 20%, implying a 23.4% gain in output per hour. Using the pilot's microdata, released under the Institute's data-sharing policy, we re-examine the result. Four problems, each documented below, account for most of the reported gain: attrition that was not random, a manager-reported output measure that overstates output relative to organisations' own records, an hours denominator that counts scheduled rather than actual time, and an unadjusted revenue comparison. Correcting the first three, the gain in output per hour falls from 23.4% to 10.8% in the subset of organisations where correction is possible. We then argue that the remaining gain is plausibly a novelty effect, and that the per-hour productivity gains reported for reduced-hours schemes are, in our assessment, entirely an artifact of measurement, selection and novelty.

## 1. Attrition

The working paper states that nine of the 70 enrolled organisations "withdrew during the preparation phase, chiefly for scheduling reasons". The microdata tell a different story. Seven of the nine withdrew after the reduced schedule had begun: four in the first month and three in the second. In exit forms, six of the nine gave workload or inability to maintain output as the main reason, and two gave scheduling. The organisations that found the change hardest were therefore removed from the sample before the outcome was measured. With nine of 70 organisations missing, and those nine plausibly the least successful, the reported sample of 61 is a sample of survivors.

## 2. The output measure

The primary outcome was an index completed by a manager who was also the pilot's internal sponsor. Managers were asked to base the index on organisational records, but were not required to submit them. Twenty-three organisations did submit underlying records (billable hours delivered, tickets closed, units produced, or cases completed). For these 23 we can compare the manager's index with the index implied by the records.

**Table 1. Manager-reported and record-based output, 23 organisations with records**

| Measure | Mean output index (baseline = 100) |
|---|---|
| Manager-reported index | 98.9 |
| Index computed from submitted records | 95.1 |
| Difference | −3.8 points |

In 19 of the 23 organisations the manager-reported index exceeded the record-based index. We do not suggest bad faith. A manager responsible for a change he or she advocated, asked to rate its effect on a scale where 100 means "unchanged", will tend to round toward success. But the difference is systematic, and the headline output figure of 98.7 should not be taken at face value.

## 3. The hours denominator

The pilot computed output per hour by dividing output by the ratio of scheduled hours, 0.8. Twenty-seven organisations used time-tracking software throughout. Their data show average actual weekly hours of 40.3 at baseline and 34.6 during the pilot, a fall of 14.1% rather than 20%. The difference comes from two sources visible in the logs: longer working days on the remaining four days (average +0.7 hours per day), and work logged on the scheduled day off (on average 1.6 hours per week). Some further work on the day off is probably not logged.

Seventeen organisations have both submitted output records and time tracking. In this subset, record-based output was 95.4 and actual hours fell from 40.4 to 34.8 (−13.9%). The implied gain in output per actual hour is 10.8% (95.4 / 86.1), less than half the reported 23.4%.

**Table 2. Implied gain in output per hour under successive corrections**

| Specification | Output | Hours ratio | Gain per hour |
|---|---|---|---|
| As reported (all 61) | 98.7 | 0.800 | +23.4% |
| Record-based output, scheduled hours (23) | 95.1 | 0.800 | +18.9% |
| Manager-reported output, actual hours (27) | 98.4 | 0.859 | +14.6% |
| Record-based output, actual hours (17) | 95.4 | 0.861 | +10.8% |

## 4. Revenue

The working paper reports revenue 1.4% higher than in the previous year. This is a nominal comparison. Consumer prices rose by 4.1% over the same twelve months; in real terms, revenue in participating organisations fell by approximately 2.6%. Revenue is in any case a poor proxy for productivity, but the figure as presented gives a misleading impression of growth.

## 5. Sectoral claims

The pilot concluded that gains in output per hour were "found in every sector" and that the model is "sector-general". This conclusion is an artifact of the per-hour metric. When hours are cut by 20%, any output index above 80 will register as a per-hour gain. Retail and hospitality output fell by 6.9% on the manager-reported measure; the three retail and hospitality organisations among the 23 with records show a fall of 11.2%. A fall in output of this size in a customer-facing business is not evidence that reduced hours work there. The Varden County trial's counter and contact-centre stratum, the only randomised evidence on coverage-bound work, found a fall in output per employee of 11.4% and longer waits for the public. That is, in our view, the most reliable finding in the literature to date.

## 6. Novelty

After the corrections above, a gain in output per actual hour of about 11% remains in the subset of survivors with usable data. We think this residual should not be read as a durable effect. The pilot's own survey shows self-reported energy at work rising by 0.61 standard deviations at month three and falling to 0.29 at month six. Extrapolating this decline, energy would return to baseline at around month ten. A change that staff chose, welcomed and knew to be under evaluation is the classic setting for a novelty effect: effort rises while the change is new and observed, and falls back once it is routine. Six months is not long enough to distinguish a novelty effect from a durable one, and the burden of proof lies with those claiming the latter.

## 7. The meetings hypothesis

The Varden trial's authors report, in an unregistered exploratory analysis, that cuts in recurring meetings correlated with per-hour gains across seven treated offices, and suggest this as a mechanism. We regard this as a post hoc account fitted to a subgroup. A correlation across seven offices, selected for analysis after the results were known, is precisely the kind of finding that does not replicate. The meetings explanation has an intuitive appeal that has outrun its evidence, and it should not be cited as a mechanism.

## 8. Conclusion

Taking the problems together: attrition removed the organisations least able to cope; the output measure overstated output by roughly four points; the hours measure overstated the reduction in time by roughly six points; and the remaining gain coincides with a decaying measure of enthusiasm. We conclude that the per-hour productivity gains reported for reduced-hours schemes are, in our assessment, entirely an artifact of measurement, selection and novelty, and that the best-supported finding is the negative one: where output depends on presence, reduced hours reduce output.

We recommend that future evaluations use record-based output, actual hours, a randomised or at least matched comparison group, follow-up of at least eighteen months, and analysis of all enrolled organisations including those that withdraw.

## Data note

All re-analyses use the Halden pilot microdata (release 1.2). The corrections in Table 2 can only be computed for subsets of organisations, and those subsets were not chosen at random; organisations with time tracking and records may differ from the others. Our corrected estimates therefore describe those subsets, not the pilot as a whole.

response:
# A Careful Reading of the Varga and Holm Re-examination

This comment does two different things, and they deserve different verdicts. Sections 1 to 5 are valuable forensic work with the microdata. They largely confirm the weaknesses visible in the original working paper, and they turn up a serious factual discrepancy in it. Sections 6 to 8 then reach a conclusion that is not supported. The authors' own corrected data, the randomised trial they cite, and their own data note all argue against "entirely an artifact."

## Checking the numbers

Most figures reproduce:

- **Table 2.** 95.1 ÷ 0.8 gives +18.9%. 98.4 ÷ 0.859 gives +14.6%. 95.4 ÷ 0.861 gives +10.8%.
- **Hours.** 40.3 → 34.6 is −14.1%, and 40.4 → 34.8 is −13.9%.
- **Revenue.** 1.014 ÷ 1.041 gives −2.6% in real terms.

One figure does not add up. The authors attribute the smaller hours cut to two things: about 0.7 extra hours on each of four days, and 1.6 hours logged on the day off. That is 4.4 extra hours a week on top of the 32-hour schedule, or about 36.4 hours. Starting from the baseline daily length (40.3 ÷ 5), it is about 36.6. Either way, these components imply roughly 36.5 hours, not the reported 34.6.

So the components, the total, or the definitions behind them are wrong. If the components are right, the real cut in hours was only about 9 to 10%, and the corrected per-hour gain would be smaller again. If the total is right, the description of where the extra time went is wrong. Either way, this needs reconciling before Table 2 can be relied on.

## What the comment gets right

1. **Attrition.** The working paper says the nine withdrawals happened "during the preparation phase, chiefly for scheduling reasons." The microdata reportedly show that seven left after the schedule had started, and six cited workload or output. If so, the working paper misdescribed its own attrition. That is a serious finding and needs a response from the Halden authors.
2. **Manager-rated versus record-based output.** In 19 of 23 organisations, the manager's index was higher than the records. A systematic gap of about 3.8 points is good direct evidence of optimistic rating. It confirms what the original design made likely.
3. **Scheduled versus actual hours.** This is the same correction the Varden trial made, and it moves the estimate by a similar amount: from 22% to 12.5% at Varden, and here from 23.4% to 14.6% on manager-rated output.
4. **Revenue.** The inflation adjustment is correct and worth making. CPI is a rough deflator for business revenue, but the point stands.
5. **Sector claims.** The point that any output index above 80 registers as a per-hour gain is correct. The record-based retail figure of −11.2% supports it, although it rests on only three organisations.
6. **The data note.** It honestly says the corrected estimates describe non-random subsets of organisations.

## Where the comment goes wrong

### 1. The abstract overstates what was corrected

The abstract says the authors corrected "the first three" problems, which includes attrition. Table 2 corrects output and hours only. Attrition is never quantified.

A rough check suggests attrition cannot remove a gain of 10.8%. This assumes the 17-organisation subset is representative and weights organisations equally. Suppose all nine dropouts had *zero* per-hour gain: the average across all 70 would still be about 9.4%. Suppose they had a 10% *loss*: it would still be about 8%. Attrition could erase the residual only if the dropouts were very large or performed catastrophically. The authors should provide bounds like these rather than imply that attrition explains the result.

### 2. "Entirely an artifact" contradicts the authors' own results

After every correction they could make, a gain of 10.8% remains. The authors then say six months "is not long enough to distinguish a novelty effect from a durable one." If the data cannot tell the two apart, they cannot support "entirely an artifact" any more than "durable gain."

The data note also says the corrected estimates "describe those subsets, not the pilot as a whole." Yet the conclusion extends to "reduced-hours schemes" in general. That is the same kind of overgeneralisation the comment criticises in the Halden paper.

### 3. Selective use of the Varden trial

The comment calls Varden's counter-office result "the most reliable finding in the literature." It does not mention Varden's case-processing result. That stratum already meets most of the comment's own recommendations:

| Recommendation | Varden case-processing stratum |
|---|---|
| Record-based output | Yes |
| Actual hours from timesheets | Yes |
| Randomised control group | Yes |
| No reported attrition | Yes |
| Follow-up of 18+ months | No (9 months, with 24-month follow-up under way) |

It found +12.5% output per actual hour (95% CI +6.9 to +18.4), close to the comment's own corrected figure of 10.8%.

Even Varden's counter offices showed +6.7% per actual hour. That does not fit "entirely an artifact" either, though that interval may be fragile with only 5 v 5 offices. Two independent sources, using the comment's preferred methods, converge on a per-hour gain of roughly 10 to 12% in non-coverage work. The comment needs to engage with that, not leave it out.

### 4. The novelty argument is weaker than presented

- **Energy is not output.** Self-reported energy is measured at only two points after baseline. Projecting its decline to month ten is guesswork about a proxy.
- **The direct test was available but not used.** Halden collected the output index *monthly*. If novelty drives the gain, output per hour should fall between month three and month six. The comment does not report this, even though the microdata should contain it.
- **Novelty also predicts a problem for Varden.** Varden's control staff also knew a trial was running. If simply being observed lifted effort, it would partly lift the control offices too, which would reduce the treatment-control difference.
- **The burden of proof applies both ways.** "The burden of proof lies with those claiming the latter" is reasonable as a call for caution. It does not justify a positive conclusion that the gain is an artifact.

### 5. Double standard on mechanisms

The comment dismisses the meetings hypothesis as post hoc. It then offers novelty, which is equally untested and rests on two points of an energy proxy. Several of its criticisms of the meetings analysis are inaccurate or one-sided:

- The Varden authors made the same caveats themselves. They said a correlation across seven offices cannot establish a mechanism, and they registered a confirmatory test.
- The seven offices were the entire treated case-processing stratum, not a subgroup picked after the results were known.
- Halden's interviews offer independent qualitative support: 47 of 58 managers mentioned cutting meetings.
- The two explanations make different predictions. A gain from cutting meetings should last unless meetings creep back, while a novelty gain should fade. The two can therefore be told apart with data.

Saying the meetings hypothesis is unconfirmed is fair. Saying it "should not be cited as a mechanism" while putting forward novelty instead is not.

### 6. A problem with the record-based measure

"Billable hours delivered" is one of the record types used. For organisations that measure output this way, output per hour is close to a measure of how much of the time is billed. It falls automatically when hours fall, whatever happens to productivity. The record-based index may therefore *understate* output for professional-services firms. The comment should show how much of the 3.8-point gap comes from organisations using this measure.

## Overall

Sections 1 to 5 seriously undermine the Halden headline figure of 23.4% and its claim that the model works in every sector. The undisclosed post-start withdrawals are a significant finding in their own right.

The defensible conclusion is narrower than the one drawn. Corrected for output measurement and hours, the per-hour gain in Halden's surviving organisations is about 11%, and it may be lower if the hours inconsistency is resolved downward. That figure agrees with randomised evidence from Varden. Whether it lasts is open, and attrition bias could reduce it modestly.

Two findings are secure:

- Where output depends on staff being present, cutting hours without extra hiring reduces output.
- Uncontrolled pilots that use scheduled hours and manager ratings roughly double the per-hour gain.

"Entirely an artifact" is not supported. Their recommendations for future studies are sound, and the Varden 24-month follow-up is the place to test them.
